analysis.one_liner: Lets generic copies of expensive biologic drugs win FDA approval faster and more cheaply.
analysis.headline: The bill would have let generic versions of biologic drugs reach patients through a shorter FDA process, but it died in the Senate Health committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a legal pathway for companies to sell "biosimilar" copies of expensive biologic medicines — drugs made from living cells, like insulin and cancer treatments — by proving to the FDA that their version works like the original, without repeating the original's full (and costly) testing. It would also set rules for how brand-name companies can sue over patents, with limits designed to keep lawsuits from stalling cheaper competitors for years. Nothing similar existed in federal law at the time.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take biologic drugs — often for cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, and other serious conditions — would eventually pay less as competing copies enter the market. Insurers, employers who fund health coverage, and government programs like Medicaid would also save. The generic and follow-on biologic industry would gain a legal pathway that did not exist in federal law.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an abbreviated FDA approval pathway for comparable biological products, letting a competitor demonstrate safety, purity, and potency relative to a licensed reference product instead of repeating the full set of clinical studies the original required [S2] [S3].

Sets a firm final action deadline — generally eight months after submission — for FDA decisions on these applications, with annual reports to Congress explaining any missed deadlines, to keep approvals from drifting indefinitely [S3].

Restricts how brand-name manufacturers can use citizen petitions and court injunctions to delay approval: petitions aimed at delaying a pending application must be filed at least 180 days before approval, must be considered separately from the application, and a court may block final action only on clear and convincing evidence of irreparable injury that outweighs the public's interest in prompt access [S3].

Requires brand-name companies to disclose their patent lists on request and limits remedies for patents not disclosed or sued on within 45 days to a reasonable royalty, narrowing the legal levers available to keep copycats off the market [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, whose monopoly prices and patent advantages would face new competition once the pathway existed. The FDA would also take on the cost of building a review process for these applications.

drawbacks.text: Copying a biologic is scientifically harder than copying an ordinary pill, and the bill would let FDA approve copies after limited clinical testing, so even supporters concede some risk that a copy behaves differently in a small number of patients; the bill tries to manage this through a stricter 'interchangeable' designation rather than eliminating it [S3].

The bill's accelerated deadlines, preclusion of extra postmarketing studies, and limits on court injunctions compress FDA's review process, which a cautious regulator could argue leaves less room to catch safety problems before a copy reaches the market [S3].

The patent provisions only make sense with deep knowledge of both patent law and drug regulation, and some details — such as the 180-day exclusivity for the first interchangeable copy — could have unintended effects on who chooses to invest in bringing copies to market [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — a legal route to lower-cost versions of some of the most expensive drugs on the market — outweighs the costs, and the bill tries to manage the real safety risk by distinguishing ordinary copies from fully 'interchangeable' ones. The main criticism is that the pro-access deadline and litigation limits lean heavily toward speed, leaving less margin for caution than a purely safety-first design would have.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health committee, which never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Charles Schumer introduced the bill with three Democratic cosponsors — Hillary Clinton, Patrick Leahy, and Debbie Stabenow — on September 29, 2006 [S3] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, whose action history lists no further steps [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed, and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, killing the bill; the summary on file covers only the version as introduced [S2].
Congress eventually created a pathway for copycat biologic drugs in the Affordable Care Act in 2010, and the FDA approved the first biosimilar in 2015 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers came out ahead: no competing pathway was created, and their monopoly pricing faced no new legal threat until Congress acted four years later.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Senate Democrats, but the bill never advanced far enough to reveal how the full Senate or any committee would have split.

industries.note: The bill would create a legal pathway for competitors to copy their patented products, and its patent rules and anti-delay provisions are explicitly designed to blunt the industry's main defenses — citizen petitions and injunctions — against cheaper copies.

At the time, no federal law let companies win approval for copies of biologics; this bill would open that market, and the interchangeability designation and 180-day exclusivity would reward the first movers.
